**"The Fence"**

Lena had always been fast—faster than the boys in her class, faster than her older brother when they raced through the woods behind their house. But today, speed was her enemy.

She had been cutting through the empty lot behind the old Miller place, her bare feet pounding against the dry summer grass, her sundress fluttering behind her like a flag. The fence between the lot and the alley was rusted and jagged, but she had jumped it a hundred times before. This time, though, her dress snagged.

A sharp *rip*.

She landed on the other side in a crouch, her heart hammering—not from the jump, but from the sudden, horrifying realization that something was *wrong*. The air felt different against her skin. Too much air.

Lena looked down.

Her dress was still caught on the fence, the fabric torn clean away from the bodice. She was left in nothing but her thin, white underwear, her small body exposed to the afternoon sun.

For a second, she froze. Her mind went blank, then flooded with panic. *No no no—* She spun around, hands flying to cover herself, but the dress was hopelessly tangled in the rusted metal. If she pulled, it might tear even more. If she left it, she’d have to walk home like *this*.

Her face burned. She had never been so naked in her life—not even in the bath, not even when she was little. The alley was empty, but what if someone came? What if one of the boys from school saw her? What if—

“Hey there.”

The voice was deep, rough, but not unkind. Lena whipped around, her breath catching in her throat.

An old man stood a few feet away, his hands tucked into the pockets of his worn jeans. He had a thick gray beard and a face lined with years, but his eyes were sharp, assessing. He wasn’t leering. He wasn’t laughing. He just… looked at her, like she was a kid who’d scraped her knee.

And that somehow made it worse.

Lena’s entire body flushed crimson. She crossed her arms over her chest, squeezing her eyes shut as if that could make her disappear. “I—I—” Her voice cracked. She couldn’t even form words. Tears pricked at her eyes, hot and humiliating.

The man sighed, then shuffled closer. The sound of his boots on the pavement made her flinch. “Hold on,” he muttered.

She heard the rustle of fabric, then the soft *thump* of something landing at her feet. She peeked through her lashes.

A flannel jacket—big, faded red, smelling faintly of cigarette smoke and woodsmoke. It pooled around her bare feet like a lifeline.

“Put it on,” the man said gruffly. “Ain’t decent for you to be out like that.”

Lena snatched the jacket and yanked it over her shoulders, burying her face in the collar. It swallowed her whole, the sleeves hanging past her fingertips, but she didn’t care. She was covered. She could breathe again.

“Th-thank you,” she whispered, her voice muffled against the fabric.

The man grunted. “You live near here?”

She nodded, not looking up.

“Then get on home before someone less polite comes by.” There was a pause. “And next time, don’t jump fences in a dress.”

Lena’s face burned all over again. She wanted to sink into the ground.

The man turned and walked away, his boots crunching on the gravel. Only when he was out of sight did Lena dare to move. She tugged the jacket tighter around herself, then reached up with trembling fingers to free her ruined dress from the fence. The fabric was torn beyond repair.

She didn’t cry until she was halfway home.

And for years after, whenever she passed that fence, she’d feel the ghost of that shame—hot, heavy, and suffocating—as if the metal itself remembered.
